subject: Physiology
subtopic: Hemostasis, platelet plug formation and coagulation pathways
concept: Hemostasis is the coordinated physiological response that limits blood loss after vascular injury while restricting clot formation to the site of injury.

content.definition: Hemostasis is the integrated process by which vascular, platelet, coagulation, anticoagulant and fibrinolytic mechanisms stop bleeding and subsequently limit and remove the clot.
content.explanation: Following vascular injury, transient vasoconstriction reduces local blood flow. Primary hemostasis then produces a temporary platelet plug through platelet adhesion, activation and aggregation. Secondary hemostasis generates thrombin and converts fibrinogen into fibrin, stabilizing the platelet plug. Natural anticoagulant mechanisms restrict coagulation, and fibrinolysis later removes fibrin as repair progresses.
content.mechanism: Primary hemostasis begins when vascular injury exposes subendothelial matrix. von Willebrand factor (vWF) bridges exposed collagen to platelet GPIb, promoting platelet adhesion. Platelet activation causes shape change, granule release and activation of GPIIb/IIIa. Fibrinogen then bridges activated GPIIb/IIIa receptors on adjacent platelets, producing aggregation. Secondary hemostasis is initiated physiologically by tissue factor binding factor VIIa. Coagulation reactions generate factor Xa, which with factor Va forms the prothrombinase complex and converts prothrombin (factor II) to thrombin (factor IIa). Thrombin amplifies platelet and coagulation activation and converts fibrinogen (factor I) into fibrin. Factor XIIIa cross-links fibrin to strengthen the clot. The classical intrinsic and extrinsic pathways are useful for understanding laboratory tests, but in vivo coagulation is highly integrated and cell-surface dependent.
content.structure: Hemostasis involves the injured vessel wall and endothelium, platelets, plasma coagulation factors, calcium and phospholipid surfaces, natural anticoagulant systems and the fibrinolytic system.
content.function: The physiological goals are rapid limitation of blood loss, formation of a stable local clot, preservation of blood flow elsewhere in the circulation, and eventual clot removal during tissue repair.
content.clinical_relevance: Defects of primary hemostasis commonly involve platelets or vWF and may cause mucocutaneous bleeding. Defects of secondary hemostasis may produce deeper tissue bleeding or hemarthrosis. Excessive or poorly localized coagulation can cause thrombosis. Laboratory evaluation commonly uses platelet count, PT/INR and aPTT together with targeted testing when indicated.
content.diagnosis: Initial assessment may include complete blood count with platelet count, peripheral smear when indicated, PT/INR and aPTT. Additional tests can evaluate fibrinogen, specific clotting factors, vWF and platelet function according to the clinical context.
content.treatment: Management depends on the cause and may include local hemostatic measures, replacement or correction of deficient factors, platelet-directed treatment, treatment of the underlying disorder, or antithrombotic therapy when pathological thrombosis is present.
